triage.name: Fatigue
triage.reason: Extremely common undifferentiated symptom; workup spans anemia, thyroid, depression, sleep and malignancy, all reachable by interview and labs.

demographics: More commonly reported by women than men
Prevalence rises with age and with the number of chronic conditions
Often the presenting complaint in primary care and in patients with chronic illness

risk_factors.text: Chronic medical illness (diabetes, COPD, heart, liver or kidney disease, hypothyroidism)
Poor sleep, sleep apnea or other sleep disorder

social_history: Shift work or irregular sleep schedule

chief_complaints.text: I'm just so tired all the time
I don't have any energy anymore
I can't get through my day like I used to
I wake up exhausted even after a full night's sleep

hpi.onset: Gradual over weeks to months; occasionally follows a clear trigger such as an infection, surgery or new medication
hpi.duration: Weeks to months; by definition concerning when it persists beyond several weeks
hpi.progression: Persistent or slowly worsening; may fluctuate day to day and is often worse in the afternoon or after activity
hpi.quality: A pervasive sense of weariness, low energy and reduced capacity to do usual activities; distinct from sleepiness or muscle weakness
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; interferes with work, household tasks and social activities
hpi.timing: Present most of the day; often worse later in the day and after exertion
relieving: Rest or a good night's sleep (partial, if at all)

associated_symptoms.text: Low mood or loss of interest
Poor sleep, unrefreshing sleep or waking frequently

pertinent_negatives: Focal weakness, numbness or trouble speaking
Blood in stool or black stools

argues_against: Decompensated heart failure or acute coronary syndrome
Urinary tract infection or renal disease

negatives: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour

atypical.how_it_differs: Fatigue may be the only sign of serious illness such as infection, heart failure, anemia or malignancy; patients may underreport it as 'just getting older'.
missing_classic_features: Clear description of low mood or sleep problems

atypical.how_it_differs: Fatigue is common and expected, especially in the first and third trimesters; it can also mask anemia, thyroid disease or depression.
missing_classic_features: Pathologic cause is not always present

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with irritability, poor school performance, falling asleep in class or refusal to play rather than saying they are tired.
Fatigue may reflect poor glycemic control, hypoglycemia or associated kidney or thyroid disease rather than a primary sleep or mood cause.
Fatigue is often driven by obstructive sleep apnea and deconditioning; daytime sleepiness may dominate over generalized weariness.

general.mild: Alert, well-appearing, no distress; normal grooming and speech
general.moderate: Looks tired, mildly slowed movements or speech, but fully interactive
general.severe: Ill-appearing or cachectic, slumped posture, slow to respond, needs prompting to stay engaged
general.critical: Lethargic or obtunded, unable to participate in the exam, appears acutely unwell

labs.caveat: Anemia is one of the most common organic causes of fatigue; a normal hemoglobin does not exclude iron deficiency without anemia.
Low MCV suggests iron deficiency or thalassemia; high MCV suggests B12/folate deficiency, alcohol or hypothyroidism.
Low ferritin is the most specific marker of iron deficiency; it can be falsely normal in inflammation.
Elevated TSH suggests hypothyroidism; a low TSH suggests hyperthyroidism. Both can present with fatigue.
Low free T4 with high TSH confirms overt hypothyroidism.
Hyperglycemia suggests undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes; hypoglycemia can also cause fatigue.
Reflects average glucose over 2–3 months; useful when diabetes is suspected as the cause of fatigue.
Elevated creatinine suggests chronic kidney disease, which commonly causes fatigue.
Hyponatremia can cause fatigue, confusion and weakness.
Hypokalemia causes weakness and fatigue; hyperkalemia can also cause fatigue and arrhythmias.
Hypercalcemia causes fatigue, confusion and weakness; consider hyperparathyroidism or malignancy.
Low B12 causes fatigue, macrocytic anemia and neurologic symptoms; can occur with normal MCV.
Nonspecific; elevation suggests inflammation or infection but does not identify the cause.
Nonspecific marker of inflammation; may be elevated in infection, autoimmune disease or malignancy.
Elevated CK suggests muscle disease (myositis, rhabdomyolysis) or strenuous exercise; consider if muscle weakness or tenderness is present.
Positive in pregnancy, which is a common cause of fatigue; must be checked in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or teratogenic treatment.
Proteinuria suggests renal disease, which can cause fatigue.
Hematuria may indicate urinary tract infection, glomerulonephritis or malignancy.

findings.finding: ST-segment depression or T-wave flattening suggesting ischemia or strain
Peaked T waves (hyperkalemia) or flattened T waves (hypokalemia)
Prolonged QT interval (hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia or drug effect)

findings.text: Cardiomegaly or pulmonary vascular congestion suggesting heart failure
Hyperinflation or flattened diaphragms suggesting COPD
Hilar lymphadenopathy or pulmonary nodule suggesting malignancy or infection

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected malignancy, interstitial lung disease or pulmonary embolism when chest x-ray is nondiagnostic
Suspected obstructive sleep apnea or other sleep disorder

findings.text: Apnea-hypopnea index greater than 5 events per hour

imaging.preferred_when: Palpable thyroid nodule or abnormal thyroid function tests

initial.why: Screens for anemia, infection and hematologic malignancy
Evaluates electrolytes, renal function and glucose as causes of fatigue
Rules out pregnancy as a cause of fatigue and guides further testing
Screens for urinary infection or renal disease
Evaluates for iron deficiency, a common cause of fatigue even without anemia
Evaluates for vitamin B12 deficiency, which can cause fatigue and anemia

confirmatory.why: Confirms obstructive sleep apnea or other sleep disorder when symptoms suggest it
confirmatory.only_if: daytime sleepiness, snoring or witnessed apneas are present

confirmatory.why: Confirms heart failure, COPD or malignancy when suspected
confirmatory.only_if: dyspnea, cough or abnormal lung exam is present

supporting.why: Confirms overt hypothyroidism when TSH is elevated
Assesses for inflammation or infection when the cause is unclear
Assesses for inflammation, autoimmune disease or malignancy
Evaluates for muscle disease when muscle weakness or tenderness is present
supporting.only_if: muscle weakness or tenderness is present

supporting.why: Evaluates for malignancy or interstitial lung disease when chest x-ray is abnormal or symptoms persist
supporting.only_if: chest x-ray is abnormal or malignancy is suspected

supporting.why: Evaluates thyroid nodules or structural abnormalities
supporting.only_if: palpable thyroid nodule or abnormal thyroid function tests

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed for fatigue without respiratory symptoms or abnormal lung exam
Not routinely needed for fatigue without suspicion of malignancy or lung disease
Not routinely needed for fatigue without symptoms of sleep apnea or other sleep disorder
Not routinely needed for fatigue without a palpable nodule or abnormal thyroid function tests
No role in the evaluation of fatigue unless pulmonary embolism is suspected
Not routinely needed for fatigue unless sepsis or tissue hypoperfusion is suspected

decision_points: Pregnancy test before imaging or teratogenic treatment in anyone who could be pregnant
Screen for depression and anxiety as part of the initial evaluation
Review all medications and supplements for fatigue as a side effect
Assess sleep quality and screen for obstructive sleep apnea

differential.name: Major depressive disorder
differential.why_considered: Depression is one of the most common causes of persistent fatigue and often presents with tiredness before the patient recognizes low mood.
differential.trigger: Fatigue plus low mood, loss of interest, or sleep and appetite change lasting at least two weeks

history: Depressed mood or loss of interest most of the day, nearly every day
Feelings of guilt, worthlessness or hopelessness
Fatigue is present even after adequate rest
exam: Poor eye contact and slowed speech
labs: Normal hemoglobin, TSH, glucose and metabolic panel
No laboratory test confirms depression; workup is to exclude organic causes

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Hypothyroidism is a classic endocrine cause of fatigue, often with subtle symptoms that the patient attributes to aging or stress.
differential.trigger: Fatigue with cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation or dry skin

exam: Diffusely enlarged, nodular or firm thyroid
Delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes
labs: Low free T4 in overt disease
imaging: Diffusely enlarged or nodular thyroid on ultrasound when a nodule is palpable

differential.name: Anemia
differential.why_considered: Anemia reduces oxygen delivery and is a common, easily missed cause of fatigue, especially in menstruating or older patients.
differential.trigger: Fatigue with pallor, exertional dyspnea or heavy menstrual bleeding

history: Family history of anemia or blood disorder
Recent weight loss or GI symptoms suggesting occult bleeding
labs: High MCV with low B12 or folate

differential.name: Obstructive sleep apnea
differential.why_considered: Sleep fragmentation from apnea causes daytime fatigue and sleepiness that patients often describe simply as tiredness.

history: Witnessed apneas or gasping at night
Daytime sleepiness while driving or reading
imaging: Apnea-hypopnea index greater than 5 events per hour on polysomnography
Frequent arousals and sleep fragmentation on polysomnography

differential.name: Diabetes mellitus
differential.why_considered: Poorly controlled diabetes causes fatigue through hyperglycemia, osmotic diuresis and associated kidney or thyroid disease.

differential.name: Chronic kidney disease
differential.why_considered: Uremia, anemia of chronic disease and electrolyte abnormalities in kidney disease all produce fatigue.

differential.name: Medication side effect
differential.why_considered: Many commonly prescribed drugs cause fatigue, and the timing of symptoms often tracks with a new or increased medication.

history: Fatigue began after starting or increasing a medication
Use of antidepressants, antihistamines, beta blockers, opioids, diuretics or sedative-hypnotics
Symptoms improve when the drug is held
labs: Normal hemoglobin, TSH and metabolic panel

differential.name: Malignancy
differential.why_considered: Occult cancer can present with fatigue alone, particularly in older adults, before any localizing symptom appears.
differential.trigger: Fatigue with unintentional weight loss, night sweats or a new focal symptom in an older adult

imaging: Mass, lymphadenopathy or organ lesion on CT

severity.mild: Intermittent tiredness that the patient notices but that does not limit work, school or self-care; normal vital signs and exam; labs may be normal or show a mild abnormality such as borderline anemia or a slightly elevated TSH.
severity.moderate: Persistent fatigue that interferes with daily activities, concentration and mood; may be accompanied by mild tachycardia, pallor or other subtle exam findings; labs often show a treatable cause such as anemia, hypothyroidism or diabetes.
severity.severe: Fatigue that prevents the patient from working or performing basic self-care; may be accompanied by weight loss, marked pallor, dyspnea on minimal exertion or significant psychomotor slowing; labs frequently show a serious underlying cause.
severity.critical: Fatigue with hemodynamic instability, severe anemia, sepsis, adrenal crisis or another immediately life-threatening cause; the patient appears acutely unwell and requires urgent stabilization.

red_flags.meaning: Suggests malignancy, chronic infection or advanced organ disease
Suggests infection, malignancy or inflammatory disease

red_flags.finding: Focal neurologic deficit or new severe headache
red_flags.meaning: Suggests stroke, mass lesion or central nervous system infection
Suggests cardiac ischemia, heart failure or pulmonary embolism
Suggests arrhythmia, severe anemia or volume depletion
Requires immediate psychiatric evaluation and safety planning
Suggests severe anemia or acute blood loss
Suggests malignancy or serious systemic disease

special_populations.differences: Fatigue may be the only sign of serious illness such as infection, heart failure, anemia or malignancy; patients often underreport it as 'just getting older', so a lower threshold for workup is appropriate.
Fatigue is common and expected, especially in the first and third trimesters, but can also mask anemia, thyroid disease or depression; pregnancy itself must be considered as a cause.
Children may present with irritability, poor school performance, falling asleep in class or refusal to play rather than saying they are tired; consider sleep disorders, anemia and infection.
Fatigue may reflect poor glycemic control, hypoglycemia or associated kidney or thyroid disease rather than a primary sleep or mood cause.
Fatigue is often driven by obstructive sleep apnea and deconditioning; daytime sleepiness may dominate over generalized weariness.
Anemia of chronic disease, uremia and electrolyte abnormalities are common contributors; fatigue may worsen as kidney function declines.
Fatigue is common in chronic liver disease and may precede other signs; consider hepatic encephalopathy if there is confusion or asterixis.

key_questions.question: When did the tiredness start, and has it been getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months; persistent or progressive rather than a single bad night

key_questions.question: How long has this lasted?
key_questions.looking_for: Weeks to months; fatigue lasting more than several weeks warrants a workup

key_questions.question: Is the tiredness there all day, or does it come and go?
key_questions.looking_for: Present most of the day, often worse in the afternoon or after activity

key_questions.question: Does rest or a good night's sleep make it better?
key_questions.looking_for: Only partially relieved by rest; unrefreshing sleep suggests a sleep disorder or depression

key_questions.question: How much is this affecting your work, school or daily activities?
key_questions.looking_for: Interference with usual activities; severity and functional impact

key_questions.question: How many hours do you sleep, and do you snore or wake up gasping?
key_questions.looking_for: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, unrefreshing sleep, daytime sleepiness suggesting obstructive sleep apnea

key_questions.question: Have you been feeling down, sad or losing interest in things you enjoy?
key_questions.looking_for: Low mood or anhedonia lasting at least two weeks, suggesting depression

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, night sweats or weight loss you did not intend?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms suggesting infection, malignancy or inflammatory disease

key_questions.question: Have you noticed shortness of breath with activity, or chest pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertional dyspnea or chest pain suggesting anemia, heart failure or cardiac ischemia

key_questions.question: Have you had any heavy periods, blood in your stool or black stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Sources of blood loss suggesting iron deficiency anemia or GI bleeding

key_questions.question: Do you feel cold or hot when others do not, or has your weight changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Cold intolerance and weight gain suggest hypothyroidism; heat intolerance and weight loss suggest hyperthyroidism

key_questions.question: Have you had any dizziness or lightheadedness when standing up?
key_questions.looking_for: Orthostatic symptoms suggesting volume depletion, anemia or medication effect

key_questions.question: What medical conditions do you have, and how well are they controlled?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes, COPD, heart, liver or kidney disease, hypothyroidism, anemia, cancer or recent surgery

key_questions.question: What medications and supplements are you taking, and did any start around the time the fatigue began?
key_questions.looking_for: Antidepressants, antihistamines, opioids, beta blockers, diuretics, antiemetics, sedative-hypnotics or corticosteroids as a cause

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink, and do you use any recreational drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy alcohol or substance use contributing to fatigue

key_questions.question: How much caffeine do you have each day, and how is your sleep schedule?
key_questions.looking_for: Excess caffeine, shift work or irregular sleep contributing to poor sleep quality

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have thyroid disease, anemia, depression or sleep apnea?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history that raises suspicion for a hereditary or familial cause

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy as a cause of fatigue and a reason to avoid teratogenic testing or treatment

key_questions.question: Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or that you would be better off dead?
key_questions.looking_for: Suicidal thoughts requiring immediate psychiatric evaluation and safety planning

reasoning_points: Fatigue is a symptom, not a diagnosis, so the workup is directed at finding the underlying cause
Duration of more than several weeks and interference with daily activities make it clinically significant
The differential spans anemia, thyroid disease, diabetes, kidney and liver disease, sleep disorders, depression and anxiety, medication side effects and malignancy
A complete medication and supplement review is needed because many common drugs cause fatigue
Sleep quality and symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea should be assessed directly
Depression and anxiety should be screened for as part of the initial evaluation, not only after organic causes are excluded
Pregnancy must be considered and tested for in anyone of childbearing potential
Red flags such as unintentional weight loss, fever, night sweats, focal neurologic deficits, syncope or suicidal thoughts change the urgency of the evaluation
Initial laboratory testing includes a CBC, metabolic panel, TSH, A1c, pregnancy test, urinalysis, ferritin and vitamin B12
Normal initial labs do not end the evaluation; the history and exam guide further testing such as a sleep study or chest imaging

easy: Young or middle-aged adult with a clear story of poor sleep, high stress or a new medication
Fatigue with obvious pallor and heavy menstrual bleeding pointing to iron deficiency anemia
Fatigue with cold intolerance, weight gain and constipation pointing to hypothyroidism
Fatigue with low mood and anhedonia pointing to depression
Vital signs and physical exam are normal apart from the findings of the underlying cause
medium: Fatigue with a normal exam and normal initial labs, requiring a broader workup
Older adult with fatigue as the only complaint and no localizing symptoms
Fatigue in a patient with diabetes, COPD or kidney disease where the cause could be the disease itself or a complication
Fatigue with daytime sleepiness and snoring where obstructive sleep apnea is the likely cause
Fatigue in a patient taking several medications that could each contribute
hard: Fatigue with unintentional weight loss, night sweats or new lymphadenopathy raising concern for malignancy
Fatigue with exertional dyspnea and tachycardia suggesting significant anemia or cardiac disease
Fatigue with suicidal thoughts requiring immediate psychiatric evaluation
Fatigue in pregnancy where the symptom is expected but can also mask anemia, thyroid disease or depression
Fatigue in a child presenting with irritability, poor school performance or refusal to play rather than saying they are tired
Fatigue with focal neurologic deficits or a new severe headache suggesting a central nervous system cause
